analysis.one_liner: Gives drug and device makers tax credits, longer patents, and reduced liability for developing antibiotics and vaccines against resistant infections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its June 2005 introduction it was sent to three committees, moved to a Health Subcommittee on July 29, 2005, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill responds to antibiotic-resistant 'superbugs' by making it more profitable for drug, biotech, and device companies to develop new antibiotics, antivirals, vaccines, and diagnostic tests. It would fast-track FDA approval of these products, extend patents, pay companies a 35% tax credit for research and a 20% credit for building factories, and use federal grants to help small manufacturers run late-stage clinical trials. In exchange, companies making these products would face sharp limits on lawsuits: punitive damages only for near-intentional misconduct, and pain-and-suffering damages capped at $250,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Drug, biotech, and device companies get lower research costs, longer patent monopolies, faster FDA review, and protection from large damage awards. Patients would benefit if the pipeline of new antibiotics actually expanded — a genuine public health need the bill cites, including about 90,000 deaths a year from hospital infections, most resistant to at least one drug.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drug and device makers; eventually patients

how_it_helps.text: The bill would give drug, biotech, and device companies a 35% tax credit for research on antibiotics, antivirals, vaccines, and diagnostic tests targeting resistant and dangerous pathogens, plus a 20% credit for building manufacturing facilities.

It would require the FDA to designate these 'qualified infectious disease products' as fast-track products for approval, and would direct federal health officials to help small manufacturers fund late-stage clinical trials.
It would extend patent terms for these products, and establish a commission to identify dangerous pathogens and recommend how to develop products against them.

The bill's own findings cite a serious public health problem: about 2 million people acquire bacterial infections in U.S. hospitals each year, about 90,000 die, and roughly 70% of those infections are resistant to at least one drug.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured or killed by one of these products would bear much of the cost: their pain-and-suffering damages would be capped at $250,000 and punitive damages would be nearly impossible to win, moving injury costs from manufacturers to victims and their families. Taxpayers would fund the research and factory credits and the grants. People buying the drugs would pay more for longer, since extended patents delay cheaper generic competition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured patients, taxpayers, and future drug buyers

drawbacks.text: The liability limits would shift the cost of unsafe products onto injured patients: non-economic damages capped at $250,000, and punitive damages available only if the manufacturer acted with malicious intent to injure or deliberately failed to avoid injury it knew was substantially certain.
Extended patents would delay generic competition, keeping prices higher for patients and insurers for years longer.

The bill's tax credits and federal grants are a cost to taxpayers with no guarantee that companies use them to bring new antibiotics to market rather than reformulating existing products, which the research credit explicitly allows.

The new Commission on Infectious Diseases Product Development would be dominated by industry: 12 of its 19 voting members would come from the infectious disease medical, research, pharmaceutical, and biological communities, with 7 from the general public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The underlying problem is real and serious — drug companies have largely abandoned antibiotics because they are less profitable than chronic-disease drugs, leaving fewer options as resistance spreads. But this bill pays for new antibiotics by cutting two corners that land on ordinary people: injured patients would give up most of their ability to hold manufacturers fully accountable, and longer patents would keep prices high. A cleaner approach could fund antibiotic development without limiting patients' legal rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2005, referred to three House committees, and sent to a Health Subcommittee a month later, where it sat with no hearing, no vote, and no action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The Infectious Diseases Research and Development Act of 2005 was introduced in the House on June 30, 2005 by Rep. Barbara Cubin with eight cosponsors split between three Democrats and five Republicans.

The same day, the Speaker sent it to three committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Judiciary, and Ways and Means — which meant every one of them had to act on the parts in its jurisdiction before the bill could move.
On July 29, 2005, the bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No hearing, mark-up, or vote ever followed; the bill's last action was that subcommittee referral, and it expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug makers kept the status quo — no new obligations, but also no new liability shield, patent extensions, or tax credits. Injured patients kept their existing legal rights, while people facing drug-resistant infections went without whatever new antibiotics the bill might have produced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: drug makers unburdened, patients keep legal rights

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with three Democratic and five Republican cosponsors — but no committee or floor vote was ever recorded, so its partisan shape beyond sponsorship is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would hand makers of antibiotics, antivirals, vaccines, and diagnostics a 35% research credit, a 20% factory credit, fast-track FDA approval, and longer patents. Much of that value comes at the public's expense: liability caps shift injury costs to patients and patent extensions keep prices high, even though the stated goal — more new antibiotics — serves everyone.

industries.industry: Medical device and diagnostic test makers
industries.note: Diagnostic tests count as 'qualified infectious disease products,' so their makers would get the same fast-track review, patent extensions, and tax credits. Faster, cheaper diagnostics would also help doctors prescribe the right antibiotic and slow resistance.
Patent term extensions for qualified infectious disease products would delay generic versions, cutting into the generic industry's market and keeping brand-name prices higher for patients.

The bill would move injury lawsuits to federal court and cap recoveries, sharply limiting both the plaintiffs' claims and the legal work they support. The public-interest side of this is the accountability the current tort system provides.
